units.text: Regional dynamic early warning model for rainfall-induced landslide in Fujian, China
Introduction

Landslides are a prevalent geological hazard worldwide, causing numerous fatalities and extensive property damage each year (Dikshit et al. 2020;Dandridge et al. 2023).In many regions, hills with well-weathered slopes and dense vegetation significantly contribute to the occurrence of rainfall-induced landslides (Kirschbaum et al. 2010;Gariano and Guzzetti 2016;Cook et al. 2023).These landslides pose severe threats to human lives and infrastructure due to their sudden onset, rapid movement, and immense destructive force.Consequently, assessing risks and implementing early warning systems for rainfall-induced landslides have become critical priorities in geological hazard prevention and control (Samia et al. 2017;Kohno and Higuchi 2023).

The concept of landslide susceptibility was first introduced by Brabb (1985) to explain and characterize the relationship between regional landslide controlling factors and the likelihood of occurrence.Over the past decades, numerous studies have utilized Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to develop regional landslide susceptibility maps (Carrara et al. 1991;Mej� ıa-Navarro et al. 1994).These studies have examined various territorial units (such as slope units, geomorphology units, and raster units), evaluation models, and indicators to assess their impacts on the prediction accuracy of landslide susceptibility.For example, evaluation models primarily include mathematical-statistical methods such as the deterministic coefficient method (Chong 2010;Hong, Chen, et al. 2017), analytic hierarchy process (Kayastha et al. 2013), frequency ratio method (Mohammady et al. 2012), weight of evidence (Ozdemir and Altural 2013;Zabihi et al. 2018), and linear regression (Youssef et al. 2016).Additionally, machine learning methods such as logistic regression (Wubalem and Meten 2020; Xing et al. 2021), support vector machines (Asadi et al. 2022;Youssef et al. 2022), random forest (Hong et al. 2016;Taalab et al. 2018), and neural networks (Aditian et al. 2018;Dao et al. 2020) have been employed.Subsequently, the development of hybrid models that combine these approaches has become a prominent topic in landslide susceptibility evaluation research.These hybrid models include bivariate statistical methods (Constantin et al. 2011;Schicker and Moon 2012), neuro-fuzzy logic, EBF fuzzy logic, and fuzzy evidential weight (Hong, Ilia, et al. 2017;Hong et al. 2018).

It has been demonstrated that rainfall characteristics, particularly the amount of rainfall, are correlated with rainfall-induced landslides.Numerous studies have explored the relationship between rainfall characteristics and landslide occurrence (Keefer et al. 1987;Versace et al. 2018).Among these studies, A prominent topic within this research area is the identification and determination of critical rainfall thresholds for landslide initiation.Current research on critical rainfall thresholds for landslides focuses on two main approaches: the physical rainfall threshold model, which employs physical methods to derive mathematical models incorporating landslide characteristic factors (Caine 1980), and the statistical rainfall threshold model, which utilizes empirical methods and mathematical statistics to analyze rainfall indices alongside the spatial and temporal distribution of landslides (Segoni et al. 2018).This statistical approach is typically used in evaluating regional susceptibility to rainfall-induced landslides, with the primary models being the rainfall intensity-duration (I-D) model, cumulative rainfall-duration (E-D) model, and cumulative rainfall-intensity (E-I) model (Guzzetti et al. 2005;Huang et al. 2022).

Previous research on predicting rainfall-induced landslides has limitations in supporting real-time, dynamic early warning capabilities.In response, some scholars have attempted to develop landslide early warning systems (LEWS).Some scholars have developed LEWS by combining physically-based mechanical models with rainfall probability indices (Pecoraro et al. 2019;Zongji et al. 2020;Pang et al. 2024;Zhang et al. 2024), particularly well-suited for forecasting individual landslides.However, at a regional scale, LEWS have more commonly employed statistical analysis methods combined with rainfall probability metrics, achieving significant success in this area (Piciullo et al. 2017;Correa et al. 2020;Piciullo et al. 2020;Wang et al. 2020;Nocentini et al. 2024).Moreover, the coupling of rainfall thresholds with landslide susceptibility mapping has been increasingly developed and refined, contributing to more effective regional hazard assessments and early warning capabilities.For example, Hong and Adler (2008) developed a LEWS by integrating landslide susceptibility with rainfall intensity-duration thresholds.Since then, researchers have increasingly combined statistical rainfall threshold models, susceptibility mapping, and machine learning to develop LEWS centered on rainfall thresholds (Segoni et al. 2015;Guzzetti et al. 2020;Palau et al. 2023;Ren et al. 2023).Nevertheless, research on dynamic early warning systems for regional rainfall-induced landslides remains limited, and the validity of existing models has not been fully evaluated (Liu et al. 2024).Different regions require tailored landslide susceptibility and rainfall threshold models.In some areas, shallow landslides caused by seasonal heavy rainfall are predominant.The use of effective rainfall models for short-duration heavy rainfall, such as that from typhoons, is not yet widespread or mature, especially with hourly rainfall data that could enhance the timeliness and accuracy of early warnings (Leonarduzzi and Molnar 2020).

In this study, we focused on Anxi County, located in southeastern China, where rainfall-induced landslides are frequent.We aimed to develop a dynamic early warning model that could generate warning levels for landslides by assimilating real-time rainfall data.Multi-source landslide data, including historical records and their controlling factors, were collected and analyzed to obtain a landslide susceptibility map by integrating an information value model with a logistic regression model.Additionally, rainfall threshold models based on daily and hourly indices were calculated and validated.Subsequently, a dynamic early warning model for regional rainfall-induced landslides was developed by integrating landslide susceptibility levels with rainfall threshold levels.Finally, the performance of the dynamic early warning model was quantitatively evaluated using warning results from six historical rainfall events.
Study area
Description of the study area

The study area is located in Anxi County, Quanzhou City, Fujian Province, China (Figure 1), spanning longitudes 117 � 36 0 -118 � 17 0 E to latitude 24 � 50 0 -25 � 26 0 N.The region measures 63 km from north to south and 74 km from east to west, covering a total area of 3057.28 km 2 .Elevations in Anxi County range from 9 m to 1589 m.Anxi County is situated on the southeastern slope of the Daiyun Mountains, characterized by predominantly mountainous topography.The geomorphological types include erosion tectonic mountains, erosion and denudation hills, and eroded and accumulated river terraces.

Anxi County lies within the subtropical monsoon climate zone, influenced by topographic conditions and variations in oceanic climate strength.The area experiences an average annual precipitation exceeding 1,000 mm, with the rainy season extending from June to September.Typhoons and tropical storms make landfall approximately 1 to 3 times per year, causing heavy to exceptionally heavy rainfall, which serves as the primary trigger for geological hazards.

The study area is constrained by natural topographic conditions, resulting in limited availability of suitable building sites.It has a high population density of 375.1 people per square kilometer and intense human engineering and economic activities.These activities include urban and rural construction, slope cutting for housing, tea plantation development, highway construction, water conservancy projects, and mineral resource exploration.Due to the steep slopes and the predominance of soil layers and highly weathered rocks, the area is highly susceptible to landslides, avalanches, mudslides, and other rainfall-induced disasters.
Data source and landslide controlling factors

To construct a dynamic landslide early warning model, landslide-related geographical and rainfall data for the study area were collected through field surveys and existing data sources (Table 1).The landslide data were obtained from the geological hazard database of Anxi County, Fujian Province.We searched and filtered 821 rainfallinduced landslide records, with a period from 1997 to 2021.During this process, records without a precise occurrence date were excluded.Nearly all of the selected landslides involved small to medium-sized shallow events, primarily rainfall-induced, distributed across Anxi County.Most of these landslides occurred in areas with relatively high vegetation cover.Most of the monitored landslide locations were near residential areas, particularly in front of or behind houses, to ensure the safety of residents and public facilities (Figure 1).

A total of 14 landslide controlling factors were used, including altitude, aspect, slope angle, profile curvature, plan curvature, topographic wetness index (TWI), land use, normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), rainfall (average annual rainfall), lithology, and distances to faults, roads, rivers, and residences (Figure 2).Slope angle, altitude, aspect, plan curvature, and profile curvature were derived from digital elevation models (DEM).TWI, a GIS index describing terrain moisture conditions, was used to analyze water accumulation and soil moisture distribution (Sørensen et al. 2006).It was calculated by taking the natural logarithm of the ratio between the upslope contributing area and the tangent of the slope angle.Specifically, the contributing area represents the potential for water accumulation from the upslope region, while the slope angle describes the steepness of the terrain.This index is used to evaluate the influence of topography on moisture distribution, where higher values of TWI indicate areas with greater potential for water retention and accumulation.NDVI values were calculated from Landsat 8 satellite imagery using near-infrared and infrared bands.Distance to faults and lithology information came from 1:50,000 geological maps, covering six lithological units: alluvial double-layered soil, volcanic rock group, sandstone and siltstone group, laminated mica quartz schist group, and granite group.Rainfall data from 2016 to 2020 in Anxi County were interpolated using GIS to determine recent average annual rainfall.Distance to roads and residences was extracted from the Anxi County geological hazard investigation report.Land use data, retrieved from the National Basic Geographic Information Center, were  categorized into six groups: arable land, forest land, grassland, water areas, construction land, and others.All landslide controlling factor maps were resampled to a raster format with a 30 � 30 m spatial resolution.These factors were categorized into four groups: geological, geomorphological, hydrological, and engineering activities.

Rainfall data were collected from the Fujian Meteorological Bureau.The study area had 57 rainfall monitoring sites, which primarily provided daily and hourly rainfall measurements.A total of 57 sites were selected based on their coordinates, and the Kriging interpolation method was applied to generate regional rainfall distribution maps for subsequent rainfall threshold calculations.Most landslides were directly triggered or significantly influenced by rainfall.We analyzed the relationship between rainfall and 70% of the landslides with confirmed occurrence times by examining the correlation between landslide frequency and monthly rainfall in Anxi County (Figure 3).The analysis shows that average monthly rainfall peaks in June, coinciding with the highest number of landslides, representing 35.9% of the total.Most landslides occurred between June and September, closely linked to the rainy season, with a notable number also occurring in March and April due to spring rainfall.These findings demonstrate a clear positive correlation between landslide frequency and monthly rainfall, highlighting the critical role of rainfall in triggering landslides.First, historical landslide data and 14 controlling factors are gathered and analyzed in Anxi County.These factors (see section 2.2) are categorized into four groups: geological, geomorphological, hydrological, and engineering activities.
Methodologies

Next, the information value model is integrated with the logistic regression model, using these factors as inputs to generate a landslide susceptibility map for Anxi County, showing susceptibility levels across different locations.

Subsequently, traditional rainfall threshold models including the rainfall intensityduration (I-D) model, cumulative rainfall-duration (E-D) model, and cumulative rainfall-intensity (E-I) model are used to calculate the daily thresholds.Effective rainfall threshold models including the effective rainfall intensity-duration (EI-D) model, effective cumulative rainfall-duration (EE-D) model, and effective cumulative rainfallintensity (EE-EI) model are used to calculate the hourly thresholds.We then evaluate the performance of these threshold models.Finally, real-time daily and hourly rainfall data are input into these threshold models to calculate dynamic rainfall threshold levels.These dynamic threshold levels are combined with landslide susceptibility levels using a fuzzy evaluation matrix to produce early warning levels.The performance of this dynamic early warning model is then verified.
Landslide susceptibility mapping model
Information value model

The information value model is a statistical method based on probability theory, which has been widely used in landslide susceptibility mapping (Sarkar et al. 2013), it uses the entropy value in the process of geological hazard occurrence to represent the probability of a geological hazard occurring.Information value is defined as the ratio of the density of landslides to the logarithm of the landslide density, and it is used to define the weight value for each classification unit.The larger the information value, the greater the likelihood of occurrence of internal landslide disasters.
I i ¼ log 2 N i =N S i =S (1)

where S is the total number of territorial units in the study area; N is the total number of territorial units in the study area that have landslides; S i is the total number of territorial units in the study area that contain evaluation index 'I'; N i is the total number of cells in the study area that contain evaluation index 'I' and have landslides occurring.The total informative value can be calculated using the following equation:
I ¼ X n i¼1 I i ¼ X n i¼1 log 2 N i =N S i =S (2)
Logistic regression model

The logistic regression model is a generalized linear regression method commonly used in statistics for analyzing binary variables (Baharvand et al. 2020).It can map the results to the range of [0, 1] through an activation function.It is mainly used to develop an optimal fitting function between a dependent variable and multiple independent variables.It has been widely applied in spatial prediction of landslide disasters.The susceptibility of landslides is evaluated based on the probability values of landslide occurrence, and landslide susceptibility is defined as follows:
P ¼ e Y 1 þ e Y
where P represents the probability of landslide occurrence; Y represents the linear regression equation and can be defined as the following equation:
Y ¼ ln P 1 − P � � ¼ b 1 x 1 þ b 2 x 2 þ � � � þ b n x n þ a (4)
where a, n, b i , and x i represent the intercept, the number of variables, the regression coefficient of variable x i , and the variable factors controlling the landslide occurrence.
Theory of critical rainfall thresholds
Early effective rainfall theory

Early rainfall can increase the water content in the slope soil, raise the groundwater level, and increase the pore water pressure, thereby diminishing slope stability.Under the influence of external triggering factors, landslides can occur.Some scholars believe that under the influence of early rainfall, the daily rainfall threshold for landslide initiation would be appropriately reduced.The rainfall in the 15 days before the landslide shows the strongest correlation with landslide occurrence.The equation for the effective rainfall model is as follows (Wu et al. 2014):
R c ¼ R 0 þ aR 1 þ a 2 R 2 þ � � � þ a n R n (5)

where R c is the effective rainfall for n days before landslide occurrence; R 0 is the rainfall on the day of landslide occurrence; R n is the daily rainfall for n days before landslide occurrence; a is the coefficient of the effect of rainfall on landslide in the model in the previous period; and n is the number of days experienced by the landslide occurrence.
Rainfall intensity-duration (I-D) model

Since Caine (1980) first proposed using the relationship expression between rainfall intensity and rainfall duration to represent rainfall thresholds when studying the triggering relationship between landslides and rainfall, scholars both domestically and internationally have conducted extensive research using the I-D model.The expression for this model is as follows:
I ¼ aD −b þ c (6

where I is the rainfall intensity.It can be the average rainfall intensity or the peak rainfall intensity.D is the duration of rainfall, a and b are coefficients of the I-D rainfall threshold model, and c is a constan t � 0.
Cumulative rainfall-duration (E-D) model

The E-D (Peruccacci et al. 2017) model constructs a rainfall threshold model for landslides based on the relationship expression between cumulative rainfall and rainfall duration.The expression for the model is as follows:
E ¼ aD −b þ c (7)
where E is the cumulative rainfall during the rainfall period, and D is the duration of rainfall.a and b are coefficients of the E-D rainfall threshold model, and c is a constan t � 0.
Cumulative rainfall-intensity (E-I) model

The E-I model constructs a landslide rainfall threshold model based on the relationship between cumulative rainfall and rainfall intensity.The expression is as follows.where E is the cumulative rainfall during the rainfall period, and I is the rainfall intensity during the rainfall period.It can be the average rainfall intensity or the peak rainfall intensity.a and b are coefficients of the E-I rainfall threshold model, and c is a constan t � 0.

Effective rainfall threshold model

The effective rainfall threshold model includes cumulative effective rainfall intensityduration (EI-D), cumulative effective rainfall-duration (EE-D), and cumulative effective rainfall-cumulative effective rainfall intensity (EE-EI) models, which have identical model expression based on the three formulas above [Equations ( 6)-( 8)].In these models, EE and EI are calculated from E and I according to the early effective rainfall theory (Huang et al. 2022).
Landslide early warning based on susceptibility map and rainfall thresholds

To integrate the landslide susceptibility map with the rainfall threshold model for dynamic early warning, the proposed confusion matrix (Table 2) is based on a fundamental assumption: as rainfall severity increases, landslides may be triggered even at lower susceptibility levels (Segoni et al. 2015).To construct the dynamic landslide early warning model, the landslide susceptibility map was divided into five intervals using the natural breaks method in GIS: very low susceptibility zone (S1), low susceptibility zone (S2), moderate susceptibility zone (S3), high susceptibility zone (S4), and very high susceptibility zone (S5).Critical rainfall threshold levels were defined as R1, R2, R3, R4, and R5, corresponding to probabilities of rainfall-induced landslides of 0-10%, 10-30%, 30-50%, 50-80%, and 80-100%, respectively.These five susceptibility levels (S1-S5) were then combined with real-time rainfall threshold levels (R1-R5) through a confusion matrix to generate landslide hazard warning levels (H1-H5), representing warning levels from very low to very high.As warning levels increase in landslide hazard zones, the probability of landslide occurrence also rises, necessitating corresponding geological hazard prevention and control measures.
Development and validation of dynamic early warning model
Landslide susceptibility mapping

Fourteen landslide controlling factors were used and evaluated using grid units.The factors were then resampled to a 30 � 30 m resolution using GIS, producing 3,366,317 grid cells for further analysis.Following a search and filter process, 821 rainfallinduced landslide records were selected.To obtain the optimal landslide susceptibility map, we extensively discussed this issue in a previous publication (Dou et al. 2023).

In that study, we compared different methods for generating non-landslide points, combined with various machine learning models, and evaluated their performance using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and area under the curve (AUC) values.We found that the best-performing susceptibility map used low-susceptibility intervals from the information value model to generate non-landslide points, combined with a logistic regression model.This approach achieved the highest AUC value and demonstrated strong generalization ability.First, we applied the Gini coefficient method to assess the contribution of all controlling factors to landslides, discarding those that did not contribute positively.The selected 14 factor layers were analyzed using GIS (see Figure 2).The information value for each interval was calculated using the information value model with the weighted overlay tool.Low-susceptibility areas were used to generate 821 random non-landslide points, matching the number of landslide points.The landslide and non-landslide datasets were divided into training and testing subsets (70/30) using stratified sampling, with landslides labeled as '1' and non-landslides as '0'.The training dataset (70%) was used to train a logistic regression model.The optimal landslide susceptibility map for Anxi was then obtained by applying the model across all regions using GIS.The susceptibility map was classified into five levels using the natural breaks method: very low (S1), low (S2), moderate (S3), high (S4), and very high (S5) susceptibility zones, as shown in Figure 5. District statistics are provided in Table 3, and it is evident that as susceptibility increases, the proportion of landslides rises significantly, with 79% of the landslides located in the high (S4) and very high (S5) susceptibility zones.Therefore, this map was used in the development of the dynamic early warning model.
Determination of landslide rainfall thresholds

The empirical rainfall threshold model identifies landslide triggers by calculating optimal landslide rainfall days and rainfall coefficients.Various threshold models, including I-D, E-D, E-I, EI-D, EE-D, and EE-EI were developed and evaluated for their effectiveness.

To define rainfall thresholds, previous research on threshold curve fitting methods primarily focuses on four mathematical approaches: (1) a frequentist least square method, (2) a frequentist quantile regression method, (3) a Bayesian quantile regression method, and (4) a machine-learning symbolic regression method (Ning et al. 2023).Similarly, in this study, we applied a logistic regression method [Equations (4)], a type of approach under category (4), to fit rainfall threshold curves for different probability levels.Based on a comparison with previous research (Segoni et al. 2015;Huang et al. 2022) and an analysis of field conditions in the study area, we established lower bound thresholds for four non-exceedance probability levels: p ¼ 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8.Consequently, rainfall thresholds are classified into five levels according to landslide occurrence probability: very low (R1 � 10%), low (R2: 10-30%), moderate (R3: 30-50%), high (R4: 50-80%), and very high (R5 � 80%).
Calculation of early effective rainfall

For rainfall-induced landslides, there is often a lag between rainfall events and landslide occurrence.Rainfall that triggers landslides typically involves two stages: (1) the antecedent rainfall stage, where initial rainfall infiltration is reduced by interception, evaporation, and seepage, and does not fully impact the slope soil.As rainfall continues, soil moisture increases, causing the shear strength of the root-soil composite to decrease, thus lowering the slope's shear resistance and setting the conditions for landslide development; (2) the triggering rainfall stage, where additional rainfall leads to cracks, deformation, and structural failure within the landslide mass, ultimately triggering the landslide event.By combining landslide data with daily rainfall data and categorizing it according to the Chinese rainfall classification standard (GB/T 28592-2012), we found that 72.3% of landslides occur on days with light rain (0-10 mm), 8.4% on days with moderate rain (10-25 mm), 12.3% on days with heavy rain (25-50 mm), and 7.0% on days with rainstorms exceeding 50 mm.However, cumulative rainfall in the days preceding landslides shows that 50.3% of events are associated with rainstorms and 24.6% with heavy rain (Table 4).These findings suggest that landslide occurrence is influenced not only by same-day rainfall but also often lags behind rainfall events.Consequently, landslides are likely triggered by the combined effects of antecedent and triggering rainfall.Rainfall-induced landslides occur due to the combined effects of antecedent rainfall and daily rainfall.Different studies use various antecedent rainfall periods-such as 24-hour, 3-day, 10-day, and even 60-day rainfall-to assess these effects.Determining the optimal antecedent rainfall period is thus essential for accurately calculating the critical rainfall threshold in a specific study area.Since not all antecedent rainfall directly affects soil stability, only a portion contributes to triggering landslides.This study applies an effective rainfall model [Equations ( 5)] to examine the impact of antecedent rainfall on landslides.Given the diversity in topography, geological conditions, meteorological conditions, and human activities assigning uniform decay coefficient values is inappropriate, particularly for slopes with thick weathering crust and significant human interference.

Based on 427 rainfall-induced landslide events with clearly recorded occurrence times, we apply different temporal scales to calculate critical rainfall thresholds.First, the rainfall on the day of the landslide event is labeled as Rd1, with cumulative rainfall for the preceding n days labeled sequentially as Rd2 through Rd10.Second, considering local emergency response conditions and timing requirements, an 8-hour interval is used for hourly early warnings in the study area.Here, rainfall in the eight hours preceding a landslide is labeled as Rh1, with cumulative rainfall for the preceding 8n hours labeled sequentially as Rh2 through Rh10.Cumulative effective rainfall is referred to as the 'rainfall factor', while the frequency of landslide occurrences is considered the 'time factor'.Correlation analyses are conducted between different effective rainfall coefficients and landslide incidence (see Figure 6a and b).

As shown in Figure 6a, the correlation with landslide occurrence peaks when a ¼ 1 and the rainfall duration is 6 days, suggesting that a ¼ 1 is the optimal coefficient for daily rainfall in the study area and that a 6-day rainfall period may be best for predicting landslides.In Figure 6b, the correlation between antecedent effective rainfall and landslides is highest when a ¼ 0.5 and the rainfall duration is either 24 or 32 h.This indicates that a ¼ 0.5 is optimal for the 8-hour early warning model in this area.Comparing the correlations for 24-hour and 32-hour durations, we find that the correlation is generally stronger with a 32-hour duration, suggesting that 32 h may be the ideal antecedent period for the 8-hour early warning model in predicting rainfallinduced landslides.
Critical rainfall thresholds based on daily rainfall index

Out of the 427 rainfall-induced landslides recorded in the study area, 70% of the data was used to calculate the critical rainfall threshold, while the remaining 30% was used to verify the threshold model and support dynamic early warning for landslide disasters.Effective rainfall was calculated using Equations ( 5), with a rainfall coefficient a was determined to be 1.Therefore, the effective rainfall equaled the cumulative rainfall before the event.By considering the cumulative rainfall and the number of rainfall duration D before the occurrence of the landslide, the rainfall intensity I is calculated.

The I-D and E-D threshold curves were fitted for different probabilities using the logarithm of the rainfall duration (D) before landslide occurrence as the x-axis, and the logarithms of average rainfall intensity (I) and cumulative rainfall (E) as the y-axis (Figure 7a and b).Additionally, the E-I threshold curve was fitted using the logarithm of cumulative rainfall (E) as the y-axis and the logarithm of average rainfall intensity (I) as the x-axis (Figure 7c).The fitted results of the rainfall thresholds for three different probabilities were presented in Table 5.It is important to note that rainfall-induced landslides often occur in clusters, and data from each rainfall monitoring point may correspond to multiple landslides.Consequently, some landslides experience the same rainfall duration and amount, resulting in overlapping phenomena in the figures.
Critical rainfall thresholds based on hourly rainfall index

To enhance the timeliness of early warnings for rainfall-induced landslides, hourly rainfall data was used for threshold modeling in the study area.Based on the previously proposed and analyzed methods, 69 instances of rainfall-induced landslide data from 2015 onward were selected to develop an hourly rainfall threshold curve.A rainfall coefficient of 0.5 was determined to maximize the correlation between   antecedent effective rainfall and landslide occurrences.Using this coefficient, effective rainfall and effective rainfall intensity (EI) were calculated in conjunction with the duration of antecedent rainfall.The logarithm of the rainfall duration (D) before landslide occurrence was plotted on the x-axis, while the logarithms of average effective rainfall intensity (EI) and cumulative effective rainfall (EE) were plotted on the y-axis.Using the classification table of critical rainfall threshold levels, threshold curves for EI-D and EE-D were fitted to determine different probabilities (Figure 8a and b).To further analyze the relationship between cumulative effective rainfall (EE) and average effective rainfall intensity (EI), the EE-EI threshold curve was fitted for various probabilities (Figure 8c).The fitting results for three rainfall threshold probabilities were presented in Table 6.
Evaluation of rainfall threshold model performance

To assess the accuracy of the three rainfall threshold models based on daily rainfall index, the remaining 30% of landslide data was input into the I-D, E-D, and E-I threshold models separately.The distribution results are shown in Figure 9d-f.In the E-D threshold verification graph, 76.27% of landslide data fall in regions with a landslide probability above 50%, outperforming 71.19% in the I-D graph and 72.88% in the E-I graph.Additionally, only 5.93% of landslide data in the E-D graph is in regions with a probability lower than 30%, better than the 15.25% in the I-D graph and the 13.56% in the E-I graph.These results indicate that the E-D threshold model has higher prediction accuracy compared to the I-D and E-I models.Therefore, the E-D model will be used for subsequent daily landslide dynamic early warnings.The findings suggest that a 6-day rainfall duration is optimal for triggering landslides, with high risk observed at rainfall amounts of 78.49 and 133.90 mm.

Additionally, the accuracy of the rainfall threshold models based on the hourly rainfall index was evaluated.Nine sets of landslide data not used in model development were input into the EI-D, EE-D, and EE-EI models.The distribution results are shown in Figure 10.Some landslides have identical durations and rainfall amounts, resulting in overlapping regions on the graph.In the EI-D, EE-D, and EE-EI models, 6 cases fall within the 30%-50% probability region, and 3 cases exceed the 80% probability region.This suggests that all three models have similar predictive capabilities for rainfall-induced landslides in Anxi County, although the overall accuracy remains relatively low.Further research is needed to integrate additional methodologies for landslide early warning and prediction.Based on these findings, the EE-D model was selected for subsequent hourly dynamic early warnings.
Rainfall-induced landslide dynamic early warning in Anxi County
Modelling based on daily and hourly rainfall indices

For six historical rainfall-induced landslide events, data from 57 rainfall monitoring stations was interpolated using GIS software to generate rainfall data across the entire area.Effective rainfall was calculated for each grid cell, followed by calculations of effective cumulative rainfall and rainfall duration.These values were then input into the rainfall threshold model to determine the time probability and probability level    for each grid cell, the more effective E-D (daily index) and EE-D (hourly index) models were coupled with the landslide susceptibility map to enable dynamic early warning for landslides, following the grading outlined in Table 2. To verify the reliability of this model, thirty-two rainfall-induced landslides, which were not previously included in the critical rainfall threshold modeling, were selected for effectiveness verification through daily and hourly updates.The landslide susceptibility map was integrated with rainfall thresholds according to the landslide early warning grading table .Based on the previous discussion, the E-D model was used for the daily rainfall index, while the EE-D model is used for the hourly rainfall index.The results are presented in Figure 9a-f.Additionally, to evaluate the performance of the dynamic early warning model, the ROC curve was introduced for a comprehensive assessment.This method considers multi-level early warning results across all units and the binary outcome of landslide occurrences within each unit (Liu et al. 2024).The number of grids for each warning level was tallied, and the proportions of warning levels (P w ) and landslide numbers (P l ) were calculated.The ROC curve was then plotted, and the AUC values were determined, as shown in Table 7 and Figure 10.
Evaluation of landslide dynamic early warning model

For the early warning results based on the daily index, on September 19, 2016, 21 landslides occurred in the H3, H4, and H5 warning zones, accounting for 91.3% of the landslides that day, while these zones represented only 19.63% of the total area.Landslides also occurred in the H2 and H1 zones, with no landslides in the H0 zone (Figure 9a).On October 7, 2016, three landslides occurred in the H4, H3, and H2 zones, covering 24.72% of the total area (Figure 9b).On June 20, 2017, six landslides occurred: three in the H5 zone and three in the H4 zone, together accounting for less than 10% of the total area.No landslides occurred in the remaining 83.86% of the area (Figure 9c).Based on these 32 daily warning cases, the dynamic early warning model produced accurate results overall.The rainfall threshold levels and warning maps can be continuously updated for dynamic warnings of rainfall-induced landslides.The AUC values for the daily rainfall index on these dates are 0.881, 0.893, and 0.923, indicating high prediction accuracy for these three events.

For the early warning results based on the hourly index, on September 19, 2016, during Typhoon Meranti, 6.64% of the grid area was in the H5 warning zone, where all landslides occurred, demonstrating effective prediction (Figure 9d).During Typhoon Megi on September 28, 2016, two landslides occurred: one in the H5 zone and one in the H3 zone, with no landslides in other zones, also indicating effective prediction (Figure 9e).However, on June 18, 2017, five landslides occurred outside the H5 and H4 zones, indicating poor prediction accuracy for non-typhoon events (Figure 9f).The AUC values for the hourly rainfall index on these dates are 0.967, 0.917, and 0.824, indicating varied prediction accuracy.The lower AUC value of 0.824 for the June 18, 2017 event suggests that the model's accuracy is lower for this event compared to other instances.These results above imply that the hourly rainfall index is more suitable for predicting short-duration heavy rainfall events, such as those landslides associated with typhoons, rather than prolonged light rainfall events.
Conclusion

This study develops a dynamic early warning model for regional rainfall-induced landslides by integrating landslide susceptibility mapping with continuously updated critical rainfall threshold levels.The model was applied and validated in Anxi County, China, a region prone to rainfall-induced landslides.The main findings are summarized as follows: Firstly, rainfall-induced landslide events were collected and analyzed, and the controlling factors were categorized into four groups: geological, geomorphological, hydrological, and engineering activities.These factors were then used in combining the information value model with the logistic regression model to create a landslide susceptibility map, an approach that has demonstrated high evaluation performance in previous studies.The influence of antecedent rainfall on landslide occurrence was subsequently analyzed, leading to the calculation and validation of rainfall threshold curves, covering both daily rainfall indices (I-D, E-D, E-I) and hourly rainfall indices (EI-D, EE-D, EE-EI).The findings suggest that the E-D model using the daily rainfall index provides the highest accuracy for landslide threshold evaluations in Anxi County, whereas the hourly rainfall index models (EI-D, EE-D, and EE-EI) show comparable accuracy.

Furthermore, we selected the more effective E-D (daily index) and EE-D (hourly index) models for coupling with the landslide susceptibility map to validate six historical landslide events in a dynamic early warning setting.The AUC values for the three daily warnings were 0.881, 0.893, and 0.923, while those for the hourly warnings were 0.967, 0.917, and 0.824.These results indicate that the model based on the daily rainfall index demonstrates high prediction accuracy for both typhoon-induced and normal rainfall-induced landslides.In contrast, the hourly rainfall index model shows high prediction accuracy for short-duration heavy rainfall events, such as typhooninduced landslides, but lower accuracy for normal rainfall-induced events.

This study highlights the importance of accurate landslide susceptibility mapping and precise rainfall threshold determination in improving dynamic early warning systems.The findings contribute to advancing the understanding of how rainfall characteristics influence landslide occurrence and provide a foundation for future improvements in landslide prediction and management.Future research should explore alternative modeling techniques and higher-resolution data to enhance the precision of landslide susceptibility mapping.Additionally, improving the quality and quantity of rainfall and landslide data is crucial to minimizing model uncertainty and preventing overfitting.
